=============== #1793
redact_observed_value: scalar observed_value fails OPEN (not closed) when tested_column can't be resolved
---
## Context

Found during review of #1791 (the #1772 fix), which added a new caller of `run_service.redact_observed_value` (`incident_evidence.py::_failing_result_layer`). The defect itself predates that PR — it's in the shared function every results-facing surface calls (REST `runs.py::_result_read`, MCP `_run_results_payload`, `alerting/builder.py::build_run_report`, and now `incident_evidence.py`) — but a new caller means a new surface newly exercises it, and it's worth its own fix rather than folding into an already-large security PR.

## The problem

`run_service.py:1068-1079`:

```python
if isinstance(raw_observed_value, list):
    show = tested_column is not None and not _known_sensitive(...)   # unknown column -> HIDE (fail CLOSED)
    ...
show = tested_column is None or not _known_sensitive(...)             # scalar: unknown column -> SHOW (fail OPEN)
```

For **list**-shaped observed values, an unresolved `tested_column` fails closed (redacts). For **scalar** values — the exact case the #1772 fix's own docstring cites as the whole reason redaction is needed (`expect_column_min/max_to_be_between`-style rules carrying a literal warehouse cell) — an unresolved `tested_column` fails **open**, and due to `or` short-circuiting, `_known_sensitive` (including its value-shape heuristic, e.g. detecting an email-looking string) is **never even called**.

## Failure scenario

`tested_column` comes from `historical_check_context`, which falls back to `check.config.get("column")` when no `CheckVersion` history exists. Any check whose config genuinely has no `"column"` key — custom-SQL checks (ADR 0019) have no single derivable column — reaches this code with `tested_column=None`. A scalar `observed_value` is then shown with **zero** screening: not tag-based, not policy-based, not value-shape-based — even on an asset carrying a hard-floor `sensitive` warehouse tag on the column the custom SQL happens to select. This is live today on every existing caller (REST results, MCP results, alert delivery), not just the new incident-evidence path.

## Fix

Make the scalar branch symmetric with the list branch: when `tested_column is None`, fail closed (redact) rather than show, unless there's a principled reason scalars should default-open that lists don't (if so, document it explicitly — right now the asymmetry reads as accidental, not a decision). Needs a regression test with a custom-SQL-shaped check (no `config.column`) and a scalar observed_value that should be masked under a PII policy/tag but currently isn't. Touches all four callers, so verify each doesn't rely on the current fail-open behavior for something legitimate (e.g. a non-sensitive scalar aggregate check with a deliberately absent column) before flipping the default.
--- COMMENTS:
=============== #1795
data-subject-rights export/erase never reach incidents.evidence
---
## Context

Found during a docs staleness audit ahead of the 2026-09-01 deploy, cross-checking `docs/site/compliance/dpia-input-sheet.md` and `docs/site/compliance/data-subject-rights-runbook.md` against the actual code.

## The gap

`backend/app/services/data_subject_requests.py` (`export_matching_results` / `erase_matching_results`, backing `POST /api/v1/admin/data-subject-requests/{export,erase}`) scans and scrubs only `results.sample_failures` and `results.observed_value`. It never references `incidents`/`Incident`/`evidence` at all.

Since #1772/#1791, `Incident.evidence.failing_result.observed_value` is a third, distinct, persisted location that can carry the same kind of literal warehouse cell value as `results.observed_value` — captured once when an incident opens or gets a fresh occurrence, and (unlike `results`) **not covered by the retention purge sweep** either (grepped `backend/app/services/retention.py` and `worker/tasks.py` — no hits for "evidence").

## Failure scenario

A controller receives a GDPR Art 17 erasure request for `column=email, value=alice@example.com`. An admin runs `POST /api/v1/admin/data-subject-requests/erase`, gets back `{matched_count: 1, erased_count: 1}`, and reasonably tells the data subject their data is erased. If that same value also landed in an incident's evidence snapshot (a suite with a check on the `email` column that once failed), the value is **still there**, readable via `get_incident` (REST/MCP) indefinitely — the erasure response gives no signal that this happened.

## Current mitigation

Docs now disclose this explicitly rather than overclaim coverage (`data-subject-rights-runbook.md` §0 and §5, `dpia-input-sheet.md`'s Class 1 table) — this issue is the code-side fix that closes the gap the docs describe.

## Fix

Extend `export_matching_results`/`erase_matching_results` to also scan `Incident.evidence` for workspace incidents, using the same `(column, value)` match logic already applied to `results.observed_value`'s shapes, and scrub in place the same way `redact_stale_incident_evidence.py` (#1772) already knows how to rewrite `Incident.evidence` in place. Update `matched_count`/`erased_count` to include incident hits, and extend the §4 exercise steps + the runbook's disclosed limits once fixed.
--- COMMENTS:
=============== #1792
incident_evidence: N+1 historical_check_context query per failing result in a run
---
## Context

Filed during review of #1791 (the #1772 fix). Two independent review passes (an efficiency/reuse pass and a correctness pass) both flagged the same shape.

## The problem

`incident_evidence.py::_failing_result_layer` calls:

```python
tested_column, _expectation_type = run_service.historical_check_context(
    session, [result], {check.id: check}
).get(result.id, (None, None))
```

once **per failing result**, invoked from `incident_service.py::_sync_incidents_for_run`'s per-result loop (via `open_or_attach_incident` → `build_evidence`). `historical_check_context` unconditionally issues a `CheckVersion` query when `check_ids` is non-empty, so a run with N failing checks issues N separate `CheckVersion` queries instead of one batched `IN (...)` query.

Every other call site in the codebase resolves this **once per run**, over the whole `results` list, then does O(1) dict lookups:
- `backend/app/api/v1/runs.py:309` — `context = svc.historical_check_context(db, results, checks)` once, then `context.get(r.id, ...)` per result.
- `backend/app/mcp/server.py` — same shape.

`_failing_result_layer` also re-derives `suite` (`session.get(Suite, run.suite_id)`) and `tags` per call, where every sibling site resolves these once at the top of the enclosing function and threads them down as parameters.

## Impact

Bounded by the number of failing checks in one run (typically small), so not a scaling emergency, but a real avoidable cost that grows with the size of a table-wide outage (exactly the case `_sibling_checks_layer` exists to describe — many checks failing together).

## Fix

Lift `historical_check_context` (and `suite`/`tested_column`) resolution to `_sync_incidents_for_run`, batched once over all failing results in the run, and thread the resolved values down through `open_or_attach_incident` → `build_evidence` → `_failing_result_layer`, matching the pattern already established in `runs.py`/`mcp/server.py`.

## Also noted, lower priority

`incident_evidence.py`'s new redaction call path has no regression test exercising an exception thrown *inside* `_failing_result_layer`'s redaction branch (the existing `test_raising_layer_degrades_to_none_other_layers_intact` monkeypatches a different layer). No live producer currently writes a non-dict `observed_value`, so this is speculative — worth a test if this area is touched again.
--- COMMENTS:
=============== #1729
bug(core): jsonsafe.sanitize_json sanitizes dict values but not dict keys — latent JSONB-insert crash on a bytes/Decimal key
---
## Summary
`backend/app/core/jsonsafe.py:41` recurses into dict **values** only:
```python
if isinstance(value, dict):
    return {key: sanitize_json(item) for key, item in value.items()}
```
The **key** is passed through untouched. A `bytes`/`Decimal`/numpy value used as a dict key — e.g. a `{column_value: count}` metric over a BINARY or NUMERIC column — reaches the JSONB encoder raw and crashes the whole result's insert. This is the exact #1273/#1719 class the sanitizer's own `Decimal` and (new) `bytes` branches fix for values; the new bytes branch makes the asymmetry sharper. `memoryview` (psycopg-style BYTEA) is likewise unhandled — verified likely-benign for the current datasource drivers (Snowflake → bytearray, databricks-sql → bytes), so listing for completeness.

## Fix

=============== #1790
reliability(worker): verify/set explicit Celery concurrency — perf-baseline.md claims concurrency=4 but no deploy config sets it
---
## Summary
`docs/site/perf-baseline.md` describes its "production parity" measurement rig as `worker at 1 CPU / 2 GiB / celery --concurrency=4 (matched to the deployed worker)`. But none of the actual worker startup commands — `docker-compose.yml`, `docker-compose.ghcr.yml`, `deploy/terraform/azure/containerapps.tf`, `deploy/terraform/aws/ecs.tf` — pass an explicit `--concurrency`/`-c` flag. The worker runs whatever Celery's prefork pool defaults to (`os.cpu_count()`), which under a cgroup-limited 1-vCPU container is famously unreliable — it can resolve to the host's full core count rather than the container's actual allocation, or in some runtimes correctly report 1.

## Why this matters
Found while reviewing #1789 (dedicated Celery queue for `llm_invoke`, closing #1726 Part A). That fix's own doc comment originally claimed queue separation means "a long run_suite backlog no longer starves llm_invoke dispatches" — corrected during review to be precise: queue separation only prevents FIFO blocking at the *dispatch/fetch* level (a queued `run_suite` message no longer blocks `llm_invoke` from being pulled off the broker). It does **not** add an execution slot — if the worker's actual concurrency is 1 (plausible under the unverified cgroup-default behavior above), a single already-*running* long suite (this deployment class has 1M-200M-row UC perf suites) can still occupy the worker's only active slot for its full duration, and an `llm_invoke` task fetched from the now-separate queue still has nowhere to run until that slot frees up.

## Ask
1. Determine the ACTUAL effective concurrency on both deployed workers (live check — `celery -A backend.app.worker.celery_app inspect stats` or equivalent, per this project's own "only a live run is evidence for anything crossing this class of boundary" rule; don't infer from `os.cpu_count()` semantics).
2. If it's not the `perf-baseline.md`-documented 4 (or whatever the actual production-representative capacity target is), either set an explicit `--concurrency` flag on all four worker-launch locations, or correct `perf-baseline.md` to describe reality instead of an aspirational/wrong number.
3. Once concurrency is verified/fixed, consider whether `llm_invoke` warrants a reserved execution slot (not just a separate queue) so a long suite run can never fully starve it — a bigger architectural question, out of scope for this issue but worth recording as the next question if concurrency turns out to be the binding constraint.

Not a regression from #1789 — a pre-existing gap the review surfaced.

---
## Summary
`request_otp` (`backend/app/api/v1/auth_otp.py:79-104`) pads responses to `auth_otp_request_min_seconds` (default 1.0s), but that is a **minimum**, not a maximum. The eligible branch runs `is_signup_eligible` → per-email quota → DB writes → a **synchronous** `mailer.send_code()` (real SMTP round-trip) *before* the floor is applied; ineligible/throttled branches return fast and are padded to the same floor.

When a real relay (e.g. SES) pushes the eligible path's own work past ~1s, an allow-listed address produces a measurably longer tail than a non-member — revealing which addresses are workspace members. The code comment ("Only a real mail-transport failure differs") is optimistic: a slow-but-successful send also differs.

## Impact / severity
Low and deployment-dependent (floor vs. relay latency); Mailpit-local won't exhibit it. Membership enumeration only, not credential compromise.

## Fix
Send mail out-of-band (queue) so the response time is independent of transport latency, or measure-and-cap the send inside the floored region.

## How to observe (statistical — deployment-dependent, not a single-shot repro)
Requires a real SMTP relay whose send latency can exceed the 1.0s floor (Mailpit-local will NOT exhibit it):
1. Configure a live relay (e.g. SES) for OTP.
2. Time `POST /api/v1/auth/otp/request` for (a) an allow-listed/member address vs (b) a non-member address, N≥100 samples each.
3. Observed: (a)'s tail exceeds (b)'s whenever the synchronous `mailer.send_code()` pushes the eligible path past the floor — the floor pads (b) up to ~1.0s but cannot pad (a) *down*. The delta reveals membership.

=============== #1693
feat(admin): in-app workspace membership — admins add/remove members without touching env config (ADR 0043)
---
## Problem
An admin cannot add (or remove) a workspace member in DataQ. A user row is created lazily on first successful sign-in, and who may sign in is governed entirely by DEPLOYMENT ENV CONFIG: `OIDC_ALLOWED_EMAILS`/`_DOMAINS` (generic OIDC, #1386), `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS`/`_DOMAINS` (OTP — the allowlist IS the member list), tenant membership (Azure AD). "Add Priya" = edit env vars + restart/redeploy + wait for her first login before a role can even be assigned. The Admin page manages roles of people already inside, not who gets in.

**Revocation is also inconsistent per door (verified 2026-08-29):** OIDC allowlist revokes per-request; OTP re-checks eligibility only at code request/redemption — a live `dq_sess_` session survives until TTL; a PAT never re-checks membership at all.

## Scope (user-directed 2026-08-29)
- **IdP account creation stays a prerequisite — we do NOT touch the IdP.** DataQ governs only its own door; the UI states this plainly for OIDC/Azure modes.
- New `workspace_members` table: normalized unique email, `initial_role`, invited_by, created_at. Admin CRUD at `/admin/members` (audited, G1).
- **Enforcement semantics:** DB table EMPTY → exactly today's behavior per mode (zero-migration-risk default). Table NON-EMPTY → union(env allowlist, DB rows) is the membership list, enforced per-request at the shared resolver choke points: `_upsert_user` (OIDC/Azure/MCP), `session_service.resolve_token` (OTP sessions), `api_key_service.resolve_token` (PATs, REST + MCP), `otp_service.is_signup_eligible` (both call sites). Dev-bypass exempt. This CLOSES the per-door revocation inconsistency — removal bites on the next request regardless of credential kind.
- Env allowlists demote to **bootstrap seed + break-glass, grant-only** — the ADR 0033 `WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` pattern exactly.
- **Lockout guards:** the FIRST db row write auto-imports all existing users as members in the same transaction (turning enforcement on can never evict current users); removing the membership of the last admin-role user refuses (FOR UPDATE, mirroring #1400's last-admin guard); self-removal requires explicit confirm.
- **Pre-provisioned role:** `initial_role` seeds the user row at first sign-in (new-row branch only — the conflict branch stays promote-only per ADR 0033; the Members role editor remains authoritative after that).
- Frontend: Members & Access panel gains Add member (email + role), a pending-invites view (member rows with no user row yet), remove with the enforcement-state warning.

## Out of scope (recorded)
OTP invite emails (the code-request email already reaches them); IdP user provisioning; user deactivation/offboarding-transfer (#412's write pass); multi-workspace.

## Verification bar
Every choke point mutation-verified (a gate whose removal leaves the sweep green is not a gate — the #1424-class trap); the auto-import transactionality proven on real Postgres; revocation proven per credential kind (live session, live PAT) not just per door; superuser/commit test-blindness lessons apply (#1621).

Refs: #1386, ADR 0032/0033, #1400, #412 (the wider admin write pass), the 2026-08-29 admin-UI design conversation.
